Article Title: Meta launches Muse, a personal AI Agent that can do your everyday tasks; company makes a 'promise' after Muse AI Image 'fiasco' that allowed anyone to create AI images with users' Instagram photos
Article Text:
Meta launches Muse, a personal AI Agent that can do your everyday tasks

Meta's security promise

Muse comes hours before Apple's Big event

Meta has launched a new autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) assistant capable of executing tasks such as sending emails, listing a car for sale, and booking travel. The system, dubbed "Muse" and known internally as "Hatch," reportedly serves as the cornerstone of CEO Mark Zuckerberg ’s ambitions to deliver what he calls "personal superintelligence" across Meta's global platform. In a post on X, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote, "Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you."Initially limited to U.S. users, Muse will operate through a standalone app and within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. The company that for now, Muse launches on iOS, Android and the web, with free and paid tiers, and support for AI glasses coming soon.Based on the open-source OpenClaw framework, Muse functions by linking directly to a user’s calendar, email, financial services, smart home hardware, and health platforms. Meta noted that users must manually grant permissions for each service and retain the ability to revoke access at any point.Unlike traditional chatbots, each Muse instance runs within an isolated, cloud-based virtual machine designed to emulate an individual personal computer. This architecture allows the software to execute long-running tasks autonomously in the background without requiring continuous user interaction.Incidentally, the Muse AI agent comes despite reported internal concerns regarding how the software handles sensitive personal data. The system’s deep integration with personal data has intensified scrutiny over potential safety, privacy, and operational hazards—particularly the risk of the agent executing erroneous transactions or mismanaging private information.Meta has made a strong security promise including claims of implementing additional security safeguards. According to Vishal Shah, the company’s vice president of AI products, the engineering revisions successfully brought the tool in line with Meta's baseline thresholds for privacy, security, and model performance. "It is impossible to say that there is never going to be a mistake, but every single part of the architecture has been designed to make this as safe, as secure, as private as we can possibly make it," Shah said. Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said the app runs within “its own isolated environment” inside the company’s computing infrastructure, and “never sees your actual passwords or payment details.”In July this year, Meta launched a new AI image generator, Meta AI Image, that allowed anyone to create AI images with users' Instagram photos. Also, if users had a public Instagram account, Meta automatically opted them in.Meta Muse AI assistant arrives just hours before Apple upgrades its voice assistant Siri AI for the chatbot era. While Siri AI is capable of taking some actions, it is not a full blown agentic system yet like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI and Meta AI offer. Apple is likely to launch it at its September 9 event, along with new iPhones.
Article Summary: Muse is an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) assistant capable of executing tasks such as sending emails, listing a car for sale, and booking travel. The system, dubbed "Muse" and known internally as "Hatch," reportedly serves as the cornerstone of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s ambitions to deliver what he calls "personal superintelligence" across Meta's global platform.

Article Title: How Tim Cook pushed Apple into a new era set for John Ternus’ CEO debut
Article Text:
Apple’s foldable iPhone was codenamed V68

Apple is likely to launch its foldable iPhone, rumoured to be called iPhone Ultra, later today (September 9), making the first big change to its phone design in years. The keynote is also John Ternus’s public debut as CEO following his takeover on September 1. While the former hardware executive will be known as the executive to introduce the foldable phone, behind the scenes, the push into this category remains deeply rooted in Tim Cook’s vision.As per a report by Bloomberg, Cook made up his mind around 2020 following a regional tour of Asia. He reportedly observed consumers in China and across the region carrying folding handsets built by rivals like Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies. Cook returned to Cupertino convinced that Apple had to establish a presence in the emerging segment.Citing insiders familiar with the discussions, Bloomberg noted that Cook became the earliest and most vocal supporter of the category, urging engineers to speed up their work. But interestingly, Apple’s hardware labs had actually been researching flexible glass, hinges and folding screens long before Samsung rolled out the original Galaxy Fold back in 2019.The project, however, lacked decisive commercial focus. Early prototypes leaned toward a folding iPad mini that opened into a full-sized slate.Cook’s intervention pivoted the engineering teams away from specialised tablets and redirected them toward building an everyday folding smartphone intended for a wider audience.Known internally by the codename V68, and referred to by several development teams as the iPhone Ultra, the project became one of the most intricate engineering undertakings in the firm’s modern era. The report also said that planners initially aimed for a baseline price of $1,999, hoping to slip just beneath the psychologically sensitive $2,000 threshold, a marketing tactic Apple previously deployed with the $999 iPhone X in 2017.Recent economic pressures, however, have disrupted those targets as due to component expenses driven by memory shortages, internal pricing models have climbed as high as $2,199 for baseline editions. Premium storage tiers could climb toward $3,000, creating a massive pricing difference when compared against the $799 entry-level iPhone or the $1,099 iPhone 17 Pro.Despite the potential for consumer pushback over premium costs, executive leadership took confidence from recent sales trends. Top variants of the existing iPhone Pro Max model already approach the $2,000 mark, demonstrating that loyal buyers are willing to pay premiums for high-end mobile hardware.
Article Summary: Tim Cook became the earliest and most vocal supporter of the category. The project became one of the most intricate engineering undertakings in the firm’s modern era. Early prototypes leaned toward a folding iPad mini that opened into a full-sized slate.

Article Title: Skullcandy Method 360 ANC review: Bose did more here than lend a logo
Article Text:
The Rs 11,999 earbuds with two very different sounds inside them

Start with the case, because you will

You stop noticing they're in

There are two pairs of earbuds in here

The rumble disappears, the rest negotiates

What the money buys

Our rating: 3.5/5

We have learned, correctly, to ignore the second name on a pair of earbuds. Some studio, some producer, some legendary audio brand lending its logo to a spec sheet it had nothing to do with. Both parties call it a collaboration and everyone moves on. So the reasonable position on the Method 360 ANC, which carry "Sound by Bose " across the front of the box, was scepticism.That's not what happened here. Bose supplied the drivers, the acoustic tuning, the ear tips and the stability fins, and the app running everything shares its bones with the QuietComfort software. Which is, more or less, everything that decides how a pair of earbuds behaves in your ear. What Skullcandy kept for itself is the plastic and one enormous charging case carved out of it. Hold that division of labour in your head for the next thousand words, because it explains nearly everything the Method 360 ANC does well at Rs 11,999, and every place it comes up short. You will hear Bose's half of this eventually. You have to get past Skullcandy's first.It's a cylinder roughly the size of a fat highlighter, with a carabiner ring up top that doubles as a pull. Tug it and an inner column slides out carrying the buds, with a click that I enjoyed far more than I expected to.Nothing else on the shelf looks remotely like it. That's clearly the brief.It's also big in a way no amount of charm quite talks its way out of. Slim jeans are not happening. The buds seat upside down relative to the logo, in slots where left and right are mirrored from instinct, and the lettering is faint enough that I was still doing a little rotate-and-squint routine after a fortnight. Skullcandy's own support page carries a five-step answer to the question of how to put the earbuds away, which is the sort of detail a design gives up about itself without meaning to.Against that, the clip isn't decorative. It hangs off a bag strap and stays there, the sliding action means the buds can't scatter if you drop it, and I never once had to hunt for the thing down the side of a sofa. Five finishes, including a leopard print I'd never buy and am pleased exists. If you're in the bag-charm phase of life, this is the only earbud case built with you in mind. If you're not, price the inconvenience in before you commit.Past the packaging argument, the hardware is very good. Each bud runs about 11g, which reads heavy and feels like nothing, because the fin takes the weight instead of your ear canal. Three sizes of fin, three of tip. Once you land your combination they hold through runs, a gym session, a flight, a long edit at the desk. Nothing shifted. None of that dull ache larger buds usually start delivering around the two-hour mark.Touch panels are broad and dependable, which sounds like small praise until you count how many Rs 10,000 earbuds still ignore half your taps. All of it remaps through Skull-iQ, four gestures a side, and the app is one of the better ones going: three EQ presets and a five-band custom curve, an ANC intensity slider, low-latency mode, wear detection, Fast Pair, and multipoint that juggled phone and laptop without ever losing the thread. The voice prompts arrived at launch loud enough to make you flinch. A firmware update has walked them back, which counts as somebody paying attention.Out of the box the tuning is pure Skullcandy, and it is not subtle about it. Sub-bass sits on top of everything, the mids fall back a couple of rows, and there's a lift in the upper treble that keeps vocals above water at the cost of turning glassy when you push the volume past two-thirds. Divine's Kohinoor is a great time in this configuration, the low end landing like a fist and the vocal cutting clean over it. This is the sound the brand has sold for twenty years and there is nothing dishonest about selling it. If your listening lives mostly in hip-hop, house or Bollywood dance production, you could leave the EQ untouched for the life of the product and never feel short-changed.The trouble starts when a recording gets busy. Play Radiohead's Weird Fishes and the bassline and drums begin crowding the guitars that make the track worth playing; by the time the whole thing opens up, the layers are stacked rather than spread. Acoustic material suffers a related problem, where the body of a guitar arrives fine and the string detail above it gets thinned out. And there's sibilance, not constantly, but enough that an hour of anything with a bright vocal starts to nag at the top of your ears. This is also, notably, the setting in which you would never guess Bose had anything to do with the product.None of which is the interesting part. The interesting part is what happens when you open Skull-iQ, find the five-band custom curve, and pull the lowest band down four or five notches. It takes about ninety seconds. What comes out the other side is a different product.Suddenly there's air. Instruments occupy separate positions rather than a shared middle, the stage widens well past what Rs 11,999 normally buys, and the tonal balance settles into something close to neutral, which is the last word anyone expected to write about a pair of earbuds with a skull on them. This is where the family resemblance finally surfaces. Anyone who has spent time with Bose's own earbuds will recognise the shape of it immediately: the same unhurried presentation, the same instinct to get out of a recording's way rather than editorialise over it.Norah Jones on Don't Know Why has the warmth of her voice fully intact and the piano sitting a clear step behind it, not smeared into the same plane. Prateek Kuhad's cold/mess holds together the same way, the close-miked vocal staying separate from the guitar rather than sharing a lane with it. Small things you would not expect at this price stay legible: the decay on a cymbal, the shift in a singer's position between verses, the room a recording was made in. The 12mm drivers were always capable of this. The default tuning was simply standing in front of it.Two things hold up under conditions where cheaper earbuds usually give something away. The first is volume. These play loud, louder than you should be using them, and the tuning holds its shape rather than hardening as you climb. More usefully, it also holds at the other end. Bass-heavy buds tend to hollow out at low volume, so late-night listening turns thin and you find yourself pushing the dial up to get the music back. That doesn't happen here; at whisper level the balance stays intact. The second is what noise cancellation does to the sound, which is close to nothing. Plenty of earbuds around this money lose low-end weight or narrow the stage the moment ANC engages, so you end up choosing between silence and fidelity. Switch between the modes here and the presentation stays put, which is the sort of consistency you only notice a week in, and then stop thinking about entirely.What none of it will do is lunge. This is the one real limit, and it doesn't move wherever you set the sliders. Loud passages and quiet ones turn up wearing similar clothes, so music built on contrast comes out levelled off. The long build on Kashmir wants to arrive somewhere, and here it takes a gentle slope instead of a climb. Orchestral material has the same issue, where everything is audible and properly placed and nothing quite swells. Composed rather than gripping. Whether that's a deal-breaker depends entirely on how much of your listening depends on a track getting bigger.You're not choosing between a right answer and a wrong one here. The default is the more fun of the two and the corrected one is the more capable, and having both live inside a single pair, separated by a slider you'll touch once, is a better outcome than most rivals manage with the one voice they've committed to. The order is the strange part. Skullcandy went and bought some of the best tuning work in the business, then buried it under a bass curve to reassure the people who already knew the brand.The codec sheet is the sour note. SBC and AAC, nothing high-resolution, at a price where high-resolution support has quietly become the expectation. In practice the tuning is strong enough that I stopped noticing after the first week, and AAC on a phone is a perfectly reasonable place to listen from. But it's a saving you can see on paper, and if you keep a library of proper files and a player that deserves them, you will bump into the ceiling eventually.Suddenly there's air. The 12mm drivers were always capable of this. The default tuning was simply standing in front of it.What the corrected version still won't do is lunge. My only complaint is that the good one isn't what you hear first. A brand this confident about sound could have led with it.The codec sheet is the sour note. But it's a saving you can see on paper, and if you keep a library of proper files and a player that deserves them, you will bump into the ceiling eventually.The bottom end goes properly flat. Metro rumble, ceiling fans, aircraft drone, the low hum a city makes without meaning to, all of it recedes. Skullcandy has never been in this neighbourhood before, and for a commute, which is what most people at this price are buying, it does the work that counts.Climb higher and it softens. Horns, platform announcements, a conversation two seats over, these come through with their corners filed rather than gone. Wind is the sore spot; I switched ANC off on runs. Stay Aware transparency does its job with a faint hiss riding along and, at middling intensity, doesn't distinguish itself from ANC as sharply as it might. The very best cancellation still lives on products costing three times as much, which is what you'd expect and no reason to feel shortchanged.Battery is uncomplicated. Nine hours claimed with ANC on, eleven without; I saw around seven and a half at moderate volume, plus two and a half more charges from the case. Ten minutes on the cable returns two hours. No wireless charging. Calls hold up in a quiet room, sound processed but clear, and surrender to a breeze.It's a crowded slot. There are half a dozen capable noise-cancellers sitting within a thousand rupees of this one, several of them with high-resolution codec support and cases that vanish into a pocket, and if those two things sit at the top of your list, go and buy one of them with my blessing.None of them assembles this particular set of virtues, though. A fit borrowed from a Rs 25,000 pair that refuses to budge. A sound with two moods, both worth having, separated by one slider. An app that does more than toggle noise cancelling. Battery that outlasts most of the field. And a case carrying more personality than the rest of the category combined, charged against your pocket space.That's not an accident. Knowing your limits clearly enough to go looking for help, then building the fit, the features and the software to make the most of what comes back, is sharper product thinking than the skull logo invites you to credit. The badge is doing work here. So is everything Skullcandy arranged around it.So, is this worth Rs 11,999? If you want the most technically complete, most compact earbuds the money can find, something else here will suit you better. If you want the pair that sits best, lasts longest, and sounds better than a brand with this history has any right to, these are worth your time. You will make peace with the case. It takes about a week, and then you will notice you have stopped thinking about it, which is more or less what happened with everything else here.
Article Summary: The Method 360 ANC earbuds cost Rs 11,999. Bose supplied the drivers, the acoustic tuning, the ear tips and the stability fins. The app running everything shares its bones with the QuietComfort software. If you're in the bag-charm phase of life, this is the only earbud case built with you in mind.

Article Title: After social media ban for kids under 16, Australia has more bad news for Instagram, Facebook, Snap and online games companies
Article Text:
After social media ban for kids under 16, Australia has more bad news for Instagram, Facebook, Snap and online games companies as it plans to give users new 'Switch Off' button

Australia wants to put feed choices directly in user hands

Australian government is deepening legal exposure for Big Tech

Following its decision to restrict minors under 16 from accessing social media websites last December, the Australian government is preparing fresh legislation that would mandate a direct “opt-out” mechanism for algorithmic recommendation systems on digital platforms. Under the upcoming “My Feed, My Way” proposal unveiled by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's administration, tech companies must allow Australian users aged 16 and older to turn off recommendation engines entirely, switching instead to feeds that display only content uploaded by accounts, friends and creators they actively choose to follow.According to a report by CNBC, the measure carries severe financial teeth: social networks, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, interactive gaming platforms and digital services failing to comply could face civil penalties reaching 109.2 million Australian dollars (roughly $79 million).The draft legislation, released on Tuesday (September 8) for closed industry consultation before being brought to Parliament later this year, requires tech firms to actively prompt every account holder with a notification allowing them to select their preferred default interface. Beyond social networks, the proposal orders developers of AI conversational bots and online video games to eliminate addictive interface mechanisms that target underage users.“This is not about giving government control. It’s about giving people control. It’s about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online. This is sensible, pragmatic, practical reform. It gives users choice, and it will hold the big tech companies responsible for inaction,” said Albanese.While major applications currently maintain varying degrees of non-curated views, including TikTok’s “Friends” tab, Instagram ’s “Following” and “Favorites” options, Facebook’s personal connection feed, YouTube’s subscriptions tab and Snapchat's split layout, Australia’s law would codify direct, persistent user selection into national statute.Australia’s regulatory crackdown lands during an era of courtroom defeats and regulatory liabilities for major social media developers worldwide. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a massive lawsuit spearheaded by California alongside dozens of US attorneys general over allegations that Facebook and Instagram misled the public about youth risks.As part of that agreement, Meta promised to introduce chronological feed options, enforce two-hour daily screen limits, and remove cosmetic surgery facial filters for minors within months. The company also wrote an open letter to TikTok and YouTube to follow the suit.Earlier this year, a Los Angeles court handed losses to both YouTube and Meta in a personal injury action that found automated autoplay features and infinite scrolling loops harmed the mental health of a young user.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who directed the nationwide lawsuit against Meta, has also warned that law enforcement officials are now targeting Snapchat, YouTube, and TikTok for similar product safety reviews.
Article Summary: Australian government is preparing fresh legislation that would mandate a direct “opt-out” mechanism for algorithmic recommendation systems on digital platforms. Under the upcoming “My Feed, My Way” proposal, tech companies must allow Australian users aged 16 and older to turn off recommendation engines.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: 28 AI-powered smart signals to be installed in Nashik city
Article Text:
The city has around 40 operational traffic signals

Nashik

:





As many as 28 AI-powered smart signals will be installed at key locations across Nashik.Driven by the Adaptive Traffic Control System (ATCS), these signals track vehicle density in real time to automatically adjust light timings based on the traffic flow. “The first of these smart signals will be installed at the Bali Mandir junction and will become operational by the end of this month,” ACP (traffic) Madhav Reddy said.Currently, the city has around 40 operational traffic signals, along with another 20 managed by the Nashik Municipal Corporation (NMC), which are either partially functional or out of service. The remaining signals will be rolled out in phases across the city over the next few months.Reddy said the ATCS automatically adjusts the red and green light durations in real time according to live traffic demand. This will reduce intersection wait time, shorten overall travel time, and ensure a smooth, uninterrupted traffic flow.“At traditional intersections, signals often remain green for empty roads, tempting waiting motorists on opposing lanes to jump the signal when police are not around. The dynamic ATCS system resolves this issue by continuously adapting to the actual road conditions,” he said.“In addition, the new signals will feature an overhead mast arm structure — long steel extension arms that suspend the lights directly over the centre of the road rather than on traditional roadside poles. This ensures clear, unblocked visibility for drivers, even when large vehicles like trucks or buses are driving ahead,” Reddy added.The 28 locations identified for the ATCS signal system are Malegaon Stand, Sarda Circle, MICO Circle, Marathon Chowk, Model Chowk on College Road, Bhonsala T Point, Parijat Nagar Chowk, HDFC Chowk near Tibetan Market, Dutta Chowk, D K Nagar, Sakal Circle, Carbon Naka in Satpur MIDC, Shri Ram Circle along Satpur Colony, Dutta Mandir on the Ambad Link Road, Xlo Point, Mauli Lawns, Pawan Nagar in Cidco, Garware Point in Ambad, Pathardi Phata (old bridge), Rane Nagar, Lekha Nagar tunnel, Amruthdham, Bidi Kamgar Chowk, Siddhivinayak Chowk, Kathe Galli Signal, Dr Ambedkar Nagar, Wadala T Point and DGP Nagar.

These signals track vehicle density in real time to automatically adjust light timings based on the traffic flow. Currently, the city has around 40 operational traffic signals, along with another 20 managed by the Nashik Municipal Corporation.

Article Title: Denmark planted trees for carbon storage, but 21 years later natural forests proved more diverse while plantations captured carbon faster
Article Text:
Image: Canva

What did scientists discover in Denmark after 21 years

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster?

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster? (Image: Canva)

Why were naturally regenerated forests more diverse?

What does the research mean for future forest restoration?

Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21 years, scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures. The University of Copenhagen conducted a rare long-term comparison of two approaches to forest restoration and found why future reforestation projects may need to balance rapid carbon capture with biodiversity recovery and ecological complexity.The study ‘ Passive versus active afforestation of agricultural land: Two decades of impacts on tree biomass and ecosystem carbon storage ’ compared agricultural land that had been abandoned and allowed to regenerate naturally with areas that had been actively planted to create plantation forests. After approximately 21 years, clear differences had emerged between the two approaches. Plantation forests had accumulated substantially more tree biomass than naturally colonised forests, demonstrating that deliberate planting can accelerate early forest development and carbon storage.Naturally regenerated areas, however, developed a different ecological character as vegetation colonised the abandoned farmland without the same intensive planting approach. The researchers also compared these younger forests with mature, actively managed forests, providing a longer-term reference point. The findings show that forest recovery cannot be judged by carbon storage alone.The plantations had the advantage of being able to accumulate more biomass early in their life due to trees being purposefully planted instead of waiting for them to come naturally as part of the process of succession. This study shows that the plantation forests have 16 times more above-ground woody biomass compared to the naturally colonised forests within a period of about twenty years. As such, the faster accumulation of biomass led to faster accumulation of carbon in the trees within the early stage of forest development. It is important to note that fast biomass accumulation does not necessarily mean that the plantation mimics all the ecological features of a mature forest.The colonisation that occurred naturally enabled vegetation to grow by the means of ecological succession without any predetermined planting. This process will take more time, but will lead to greater diversity of plants in terms of their species and structure since different plants will colonise certain areas. The Danish study showed that the naturally colonised forests were distinct from the plantation in terms of vegetation and ecology, which proves the necessity of using natural factors in the process of creation of the forest. However, this statement does not mean that plantations cannot be valuable in terms of biodiversity, but only that the structure and composition of such forests differ greatly from the forests developed without planting.The results imply that there is no one particular forest restoration approach that would optimise all of the environmental benefits at once. Plantations would be an advantageous choice if the aim is to achieve rapid carbon sequestration because plantations would help to achieve faster carbon accumulation. As for natural regeneration, it would provide greater ecological diversity as the forest develops and could contribute significantly to biodiversity. Therefore, the scientists show a more complex view of afforestation that does not include only the number of trees planted.
Article Summary: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. Scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures.

Article Title: Soon, Aussies could opt out of social media algorithms
Article Text:
Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms.

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think Australians should have the option to opt-out of social media algorithms? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” communications minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm -- but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice.”“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds,” she said.Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social m­e­dia apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
Article Summary: A draft law requiring a ‘digital duty of care’ is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week. It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.

Article Title: Gene Autry bought a 110-acre California movie ranch in 1952; a massive fire destroyed 54 buildings before he finally sold the last 10 acres
Article Text:
PC: Official website

Melody Ranch began as a Hollywood Western film studio in 1915

Gene Autry turned Melody Ranch into a television Western hub

PC: CLUI

The Melody Ranch fire wiped out much of Autry’s Western collection

After the fire, Melody Ranch slowly passed out of Autry’s hands

Old photographs helped restore Melody Ranch’s Western street

A museum keeps Melody Ranch’s Hollywood history on display

Melody Ranch after the studio years

Before Melody Ranch became associated with Gene Autry, it was already part of the machinery of early Hollywood. The Newhall property opened in 1915 as Monogram Studios, providing a ready-made setting for Western films at a time when the genre was becoming a staple of American cinema. John Wayne was among the performers whose early productions used the site. Autry had filmed there himself before purchasing it in 1952. Under his ownership, the ranch was renamed Melody Ranch and adapted to the demands of television, with several Flying A Pictures series made on its sets.The property later hosted a long list of Western programmes, from Hopalong Cassidy to Gunsmoke. Then a fire swept through Placerita Canyon in 1962. Fifty-four structures were destroyed, along with much of Autry's collection. What followed was not a clean ending, but decades of selling, rebuilding and changing use.The property was already established as a movie location when Gene Autry acquired it. Known as Monogram Studios, the Newhall ranch had opened in 1915, during the formative years of the Western film industry. Its sets were used for early Western productions, including a number of John Wayne's Lone Star Monogram films.Autry himself had a connection to the site before he owned it. His 1935 film Tumbling Tumbleweeds, made for Republic Pictures, was among the productions associated with the ranch.By the time Autry bought the property in 1952, the place had accumulated a useful collection of Western settings. That made it suitable for the new television market, where producers needed locations that could be redressed and reused without building an entire town for every production.Autry renamed the property Melody Ranch and turned much of its attention towards television.The ranch became the base for several of Autry's Flying A Pictures productions. The Gene Autry Show was filmed there, as were The Range Rider, Annie Oakley, Buffalo Bill, Jr. and The Adventures of Champion.Other Western series passed through the gates. Hopalong Cassidy, Wild Bill Hickok, Wyatt Earp, The Cisco Kid, Sheriff of Cochise and Gunsmoke all used Melody Ranch at various points. The property was not limited to television either. Feature films continued to use its sets, including Fred MacMurray's At Gunpoint in 1955, as reported.The ranch offered a ready-made Western environment, with streets, buildings and open areas that could serve different productions. Camera crews could find useful angles without having to construct an entirely new setting.Autry also appeared there with Champion, the horse who became one of the most recognisable animals associated with his career. Photographs from the 1950s show the pair on the ranch's Western street.For Autry, Melody Ranch was more than a place where productions could be made. He had accumulated a substantial collection connected with his career, including antique automobiles, stagecoaches, costumes, documents, recordings and other memorabilia. He was considering turning the property into a Western museum.According to the official website of Gene Autry, that plan changed on August 28, 1962. A major fire swept through Placerita Canyon in Newhall and reached the ranch. Fifty-four structures on the 110-acre property were destroyed. The losses extended well beyond the buildings themselves. Autry's collection of vehicles and stagecoaches was badly affected, as were his wardrobe and costumes, papers and other material. An archive containing about 17,000 recordings was also lost.Several parts of the ranch escaped the destruction. The adobe house survived, along with another house, the adobe village, a schoolhouse, a cabin and the main entrance.The fire effectively ended Melody Ranch's period as a large working film and television property under Autry.Autry abandoned his plans for a museum and the ranch entered a much quieter period. Over the following three decades, he gradually sold most of the property to developers.The landholding became a fraction of what it had been. The original ranch covered 110 acres; eventually only a small remnant remained in Autry's hands.Champion Three, rather than film production, became an important part of the property's later story. The horse remained at Melody Ranch until his death in 1990. After that, Autry sold the remaining ranch to brothers Renaud and Andre Veluzat.The Veluzat family already had deep connections with film locations in the Santa Clarita Valley. Their family had operated a film ranch in Saugus since the early 1950s, and the brothers took on the task of bringing Melody Ranch back into use.Restoration meant working from what little remained and from the visual record of the ranch's earlier years. The Veluzats used old photographs and videotapes to reconstruct the Western street and church sets, aiming to recreate their appearance from the early television period.There was one practical alteration. The rebuilt street sits slightly higher than the original version. That change was made for the camera rather than historical accuracy, helping keep the residential development on the hill north of the ranch out of shots.The restored street eventually returned to television production. Among the programmes to use the setting was HBO's Deadwood, giving the old ranch another connection with Western screen history decades after Autry's productions had ended.The property also retains a museum devoted to its film history. Its collection includes vintage automobiles, photographs, Champion's training hoop and other material from the ranch's years in the entertainment business. Visits are arranged by appointment rather than through ordinary daily opening hours.The surviving site is therefore considerably smaller than the place Autry purchased in 1952. The 110-acre ranch that once accommodated a busy collection of film and television productions was progressively reduced through development and sale, leaving only a small portion of the original property.Yet the surviving sets preserve something of the ranch's working appearance. Buildings that were once scenery for weekly television programmes became historic pieces of a California film landscape.Melody Ranch also developed a life outside film production. Since 1994, it has hosted the Santa Clarita Cowboy Poetry and Music Festival each March. The event brings performers, musicians and visitors to the ranch, alongside Western-themed displays, food and merchandise.The ranch's history is unusually layered for a surviving film location. It began in the silent-era and early Hollywood period, became part of Autry's television operation, was heavily damaged by fire, passed out of his ownership and was eventually restored by a family already familiar with the business of maintaining film ranches.What remains is not the 110-acre property Autry bought. It is a much smaller piece of it, shaped by decades of production, fire, development and restoration. The Western street, rebuilt from photographs and old footage, provides the most visible reminder of the ranch's former role. Beneath that scenery is a longer story about how quickly a working Hollywood location can disappear, and how parts of it can still be reconstructed many years later.
Article Summary: Melody Ranch opened in 1915 as Monogram Studios in Newhall, California. John Wayne, Annie Oakley, Buffalo Bill, Jr. and The Adventures of Champion all filmed there. In 1952, Gene Autry bought the property and turned it into a TV Western hub. A fire in 1962 destroyed much of the property, including Autry's collection.

Article Title: Copenhagen’s £200m underground Natural History Museum, under construction since 2019, to open in 2027 with eight galleries, 14m specimens, dinosaur skeletons, 3D exhibits and Ocean Hall
Article Text:
Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Eight galleries will be built underground

The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

The museum’s collection includes around 14 million specimens gathered over 400 years. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

14 million specimens include dinosaur skeletons

Interactive 3D exhibits will allow visitors to explore detailed digital scans of specimens. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Ocean Hall features a huge glass dome

The spectacular Ocean Hall will feature a huge dome made with 1,600 triangular glass panels. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

£200 million project has taken years to complete

Museum will sit alongside Copenhagen’s Botanical Garden

A huge new underground attraction is set to open in one of Europe’s most popular cities, promising visitors immersive experiences, dinosaur fossils and access to millions of specimens collected over centuries.The new Natural History Museum in Copenhagen, Denmark, will officially open on March 6, 2027, following a major £200 million redevelopment project that has been years in the making.The centrepiece of the project is a series of eight new galleries built underground, creating a vast new exhibition space beneath Copenhagen’s historic Botanical Garden.The eight exhibitions will be titled Universe, Earth, Life, Denmark, Arctic, Biodiversity, Humans and Ocean Hall, taking visitors on a journey through the history of the natural world, according to The Official Copenhagen City Card website.The museum has been designed to combine Copenhagen’s historic architecture with a striking new underground complex.According to architect Lene Tranberg, natural light will reach the underground exhibition galleries through skylights, while the design aims to “engage all the senses”.Inside, visitors will find concrete interiors, curved staircases and large exhibition spaces designed to create an immersive journey through natural history.The new museum connects the Botanical Garden, the existing historic buildings and new architecture inspired by organic forms found in nature.The museum says the project represents a new direction in Danish museum architecture, combining protected historic surroundings with new underground galleries and above-ground structures inspired by nature.The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including fossils and specimens documenting the history and diversity of life on Earth.Among the highlights are dinosaur remains, including a 17-metre-long Diplodocus skeleton and T-Rex skeletons.Visitors will also be able to explore specimens using interactive touchscreen tables, allowing them to rotate and zoom into 3D scans of objects from the museum's collections.The exhibitions will cover everything from the formation of the Solar System and the origins of species to biodiversity and the rapidly changing natural world.The scale of the new museum can be seen in the construction details.The exhibition halls have walls reaching up to 10 metres high, while ceilings are made using around 180,000 small wooden slats, designed to improve acoustics across the large spaces.The Ocean Hall measures 16 metres wide, 23 metres high and 50 metres long. Its dome consists of 2,000 steel frames fitted with 1,600 triangular glass panels.Remarkably, only two of the glass panes in the entire structure are identical.The museum's welcome hall is housed in a former engine house that was dismantled and reconstructed using original facade bricks and steel lattice structures.The excavation for the foundations reached 15 metres deep and stretched 400 metres in circumference.Plans for the new museum were first revealed around 17 years ago, while construction began in 2019.The project was originally expected to open much earlier, but planning permission and funding issues contributed to significant delays.The exhibition concept was developed by the museum in collaboration with design agency Tinker Imagineers, which won an international competition in 2018. In 2023, the project entered its production phase, with Event Communications winning the contract to deliver the new permanent exhibitions.Christine Wiberg-Lyng, Foundation Director at Aage og Johanne Louis-Hansens Fond, said the new buildings create a sensory setting that supports the museum's core purpose.The redevelopment will add around 7,000 square metres of exhibition space, while another 2,000 square metres will include public facilities such as the shop, ticket office, VILLUM Hall, restaurant, café and dining areas.Around 500 square metres will be dedicated to teaching facilities for school students.Collection storage, laboratories, offices and other staff facilities will occupy approximately 22,500 square metres. Overall, the new museum will comprise around 32,000 square metres, divided almost equally between new construction and renovated historic buildings.Above the underground galleries, Copenhagen's Botanical Garden offers visitors a living museum containing around 13,000 plant species, alongside alpine rock gardens and walking trails.The site also includes the Palm House and Butterfly House, located inside a Victorian cast-iron glasshouse dating back to 1874.The Botanical Garden is free to enter, while tickets for the new museum are listed at approximately £13.22 for adults and £5.75 for children aged three to 17.
Article Summary: Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including dinosaur remains.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Israel installed barn owl boxes to control crop-eating rodents without poison; researchers later found that threatened native gerbils formed over half the prey in some nests
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image: A barn owl is depicted returning to a tree-mounted nesting box with a rodent, illustrating the use of barn owls as natural pest control in agricultural landscapes. Credits: ChatGPT

The journey from an experiment to a national programme

Barn Owl in flight. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

An unexpected pattern is revealed

In the early 1980s, Israeli farmers and researchers started testing a natural alternative to chemical rodent control. They came up with giving barn owls artificial places to nest which were closer to agricultural fields. The aim behind this idea was to use an existing predator, instead of introducing a new species, to hunt rodents that could damage the crops. In 1983, one of the best-documented programmes began in Israel's Beit She’an Valley, where 14 nest boxes were installed across around three kilometres. What initially appeared to be a straightforward biological control strategy, however, soon became complicated as researchers faced the question of what would happen when owls encountered rodents that conservationists were trying to protect.The barn owl was already a part of Israel’s agricultural ecosystem, and the nest boxes were intended to provide additional breeding sites in cultivated lands. This allowed the owls to establish territories near fields and hunt rodents naturally. Researchers at Tel Aviv University later described the nest-box system as a part of Israel’s long-running effort to control agricultural rodents via barn owls and other raptors while lessening the dependence on chemical rodenticides.By the early 2000s, the use of raptors for biological pest control had been integrated into agricultural management across several regions. In the Beit She’an Valley specifically, research showed that the programme expanded from its initial footprint to roughly 300 nest boxes covering 90 square kilometres by 2007. Tel Aviv University researchers reported that thousands of nesting boxes had subsequently been installed across the country. They also noted that this approach had been adopted in the neighbouring parts of the region as well. The scale of this initiative reflected the appeal of replacing the use of chemical rodent control with a predator which was already familiar with the local environment.Another advantage of barn owls is that they hunt largely at night, when many small mammals are active, and an established pair can make repeated hunting trips around its nesting territory. Therefore, the pest-control benefit was expected to come from owls’ natural feeding behaviour instead of any direct human intervention in every field.On the other hand, excessive use of chemical rodenticides can have consequences that go beyond the intended target. For example, other animals can encounter the poison placed for rodents, while predators may also be exposed when they consume poisoned prey. Although the barn-nest box approach can be considered a good example of non-chemical or reduced-chemical control, it also created an ecological challenge , as owls cannot be expected to recognise the difference between an agricultural pest and a protected native rodent.This point became especially important in the northwestern Negev, a different study region from the original Beit She’an Valley experiment. The northwestern Negev’s cultivated land lies close to natural sandy habitats that support native small mammals, including several gerbil species. Researchers were stumped by the question of whether artificial nest boxes placed near these areas might increase predation pressure on species that were not agricultural targets.Researchers examined 14,632 prey items from 95 barn-owl nest boxes between 2013 and 2016 in the northwestern Negev. The study identified several protected or locally endangered rodents among the prey, including Allenby’s gerbil, the sand rat, Wagner’s gerbil and the greater Egyptian gerbil. The findings did not suggest that these endangered rodents generally dominated barn owls' diet. Instead, they constituted over 50% of the recorded prey within a specific subset of nest boxes. The pattern was especially notable at boxes located within five kilometres of sand dunes.Researchers then compared those owl-diet findings with trapping data from agricultural fields and nearby dunes, and noted that in extensive agricultural areas, Gerbillus rodents represented less than 1% of the animals caught. However, in the neighbouring dunes, gerbils were much more prominent. This data mismatch clarifies a fundamental flaw in the original 1980s deployment strategy: while boxes were placed near agricultural fields to target crop pests, their proximity to native terrain inadvertently converted a targeted biocontrol tool into a structural threat vector. Because owls selectively forage across natural habitats if nested nearby, this subpopulation of boxes installed along the desert-farm ecotone drove a massive dietary shift toward protected species, drawing apex predators directly to the borders of vulnerable conservation zones.This is a classic challenge with predator-based pest management. A barn owl does not operate according to a list of species that humans have classified as desirable or harmful. Thus, if a protected gerbil becomes accessible near a nesting territory, it can likely become a part of the owl’s diet regardless of whether or not the rodent is damaging crops.The Israeli experiment illustrated why reducing rodenticide use and protecting biodiversity cannot necessarily be treated as separate goals. While using predators can reduce reliance on poisons, predator management itself must be designed carefully when agricultural land is adjacent to conservation areas.
Article Summary: In the early 1980s, Israeli farmers and researchers started testing a natural alternative to chemical rodent control. They came up with giving barn owls artificial places to nest which were closer to agricultural fields. This allowed the owls to establish territories near fields and hunt rodents naturally.

Article Title: In 1990, scientists released uranin 15 metres deep in Switzerland’s Lake Alpnach to track mixing; the dye cloud stretched into an elongated streak as currents moved it
Article Text:
AI Representation: A fluorescent green uranin dye cloud stretches through Lake Alpnach as underwater currents carry it into an elongated plume. Image credits: Chatgpt

Uranin dye at 15 meters, chosen for two reasons

Carter and Okubo's shear model, not Batchelor's turbulence model

Length-Scale Dependence of Horizontal Dispersion in the Surface Water of Lakes,

View over Stansstad of Lake Alpnach in Central Switzerland. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

An effective diffusivity between 0.02 and 0.3 square meters per second

Eawag, the institute behind both studies

A container with the fluorescent dye was placed on Lake Alpnach, a 4.5 - 4.8 km² basin of Lake Lucerne in central Switzerland, by Swiss scientists in 1990 as part of a series of tracer experiments later reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research . They released between 0.2 and 2 kg of uranin at depths of 15–25 m below the surface. This experiment had a simple idea behind it but a difficult execution: to trace how a small concentrated blob of dye would spread in still lake water under the action of invisible currents. Over the following days, the scientists returned repeatedly to profile the evolving dye cloud and map its shape and concentration.Sodium fluorescein, better known as uranin, was used because it does not adsorb to suspended particles and breaks down easily in sunlight and acidic conditions. It was injected at 15 meters deep because, at this depth, it lies within the hypolimnion, the layer below the thermocline where wind-driven surface mixing is minimal. Wind-driven mixing is not the only force at work in the hypolimnion, however; slower currents and shear can still act within this layer, and it was this shear that stretched the dye cloud into an elongated streak. This experiment, referred to as the 'Alp' run in the 1996 paper's data tables, is one of eight experiments the same team conducted on four lakes in Switzerland, with basins varying from 4.5 to 220 square kilometers and with 0.2 to 2 kilograms of uranin injected at depths of 15 to 25 meters in each case.This research was published in the paper titled Horizontal Mixing in Lakes in the Journal of Geophysical Research in 1996, by Frank Peeters, Alfred Wüest, Gabriel Piepke and Dieter Imboden. The dye was injected instantaneously and the cloud was tracked by integrating many vertical profiles over time. The paper reports cloud areas ranging from 3 × 10² to 3 × 10⁵ m², with effective horizontal diffusivities of 0.02 to 0.3 m² s⁻¹ and no support for the Batchelor inertial‑subrange prediction.Rather than expanding into a neat, ever-widening circle, the patch stretched into an elongated streak as it drifted and the same asymmetry showed up across all eight trials in the study. The scientists made a comparison between the cloud growth that was observed and two different theories, Batchelor's 1950 theory of turbulence of the inertial subrange type for horizontal diffusion and the shear-diffusion theory based on the work of Carter & Okubo (1965). The data were inconsistent with Batchelor's prediction, while the shear-diffusion theory fit the observations better. These tracer cloud sizes, which increased from about 300 to 300,000 m2 throughout the experiment, did not increase with time in accordance with Batchelor’s inertial subrange theory. Rather, a shear diffusion model proved very applicable and provided the answer to why these clouds were never radially symmetric; the reason is that the currents on one side of the cloud moved at a different speed/direction compared to those on the opposite side of the cloud.In another study, this time with drifters rather than dyes in Lake Constance, Frank Peeters and Hilmar Hofmann confirmed the hypothesis. According to Frank Peeters and Hilmar Hofmann's article "" published in Limnology and Oceanography in 2015 and listed on the University of Konstanz's publication page, constant shear in a current causes the dispersion coefficient to increase linearly with the size of the moving cloud. As reported in the study, the dispersion coefficients ranged from 0.01 to 0.03 square meters per second at a length scale of 100 meters, and from 0.1 to 0.7 square meters per second at a length scale of 1,000 meters. However, this linear relationship describes an idealized case of constant shear; when the researchers analyzed their actual field data, the model showed clear limitations.Shear accounted for less than 40% of the scale dependence between 100 and 1,000 meters. It seems that the process of turbulent diffusion accounted for the scale-dependence effect greatly and that the shear influenced only the orientation of the drifting clouds. As stated in the paper, drifters were deployed in Lake Constance in four experiments, with groups of 14 to 17 drifters spanning length scales from 30 to 3,000 meters. As stated by the researchers, the dispersion coefficient had oscillatory properties and could be explained by shear diffusion and basin-scale seiching and not by a length-scale law.For all eight deployments, including the Alpnach deployment, the 1996 paper mentioned above computed effective horizontal diffusivities in the range of 0.02 to 0.3 square meters per second, numbers that were many orders of magnitude higher than the diffusivity due to molecular diffusion alone. After subtracting the effect of velocity shear from the total diffusivity, the estimated turbulent diffusivity fell to 0.02 to 0.18 square meters per second.The Alpnach experiment is a useful example because a measured mass of dye was placed at a known depth and left to the lake's natural processes. In addition, the results showed long before the advent of satellite tracking or drifters that even a small group of researchers could obtain useful data on mixing using only dye and a fluorometer. Eawag, the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology, employed the authors of both papers discussed here and continues to run comparable lake research today, now paired with sensors and modeling tools that reduce the need for repeated manual sampling. From a garage experiment to the Morey Boogie

Why the Boogie Board name still lives on

A leftover piece of foam, an electric carving knife, and a surfer were all Tom Morey needed to create what would become one of surfing’s most recognisable inventions. In 1971, Morey was living in Kona, Hawaii, where he was experimenting with the idea of a small and lightweight craft that could offer a different way to ride waves. He was already an accomplished stand-up surfer, but he kept looking for new possibilities.According to the California Surf Museum, Morey took a piece of polyethylene foam from his garage and cut it into shape with an electric carving knife. He then used his wife’s iron to seal the foam. A copy of the Honolulu Advertiser newspaper left its imprint on the board, giving Morey a way to remember the date: July 7, 1971. That simple experiment would go on to become the Morey Boogie and help shape the modern bodyboard.Morey’s creation was different from the hard surfboards he knew. The modern bodyboard was a soft and flexible piece of foam designed to be ridden while lying on the belly. Morey found that the board allowed him to feel the movement of the wave in a way that a conventional surfboard did not. He saw several advantages in his new creation. It could turn, was durable and lightweight, and could be produced cheaply. Morey also believed it was safe.The idea was simple enough to turn into a do-it-yourself kit that people could assemble at home.The first kits came with two pieces of foam that had to be glued together along with skins for the top and bottom. Morey placed an advertisement in Surfer magazine, and orders soon began arriving.Morey initially considered calling his invention SNAKE (Side, Navel, Arm, Knee, and Elbow). The name was an acronym for the parts of the body used while riding it. But the idea was rejected, and he eventually chose the name Morey Boogie.The name came from Morey’s love of jazz and a style of swing music which was popular before the Second World War. He felt that ‘Boogie’ captured the movement of the new craft.The first production of the Morey Boogie reached the market in 1975. By 1977, the Carlsbad-based company was producing about 80,000 boards a year. In 1979, toy company Kransco purchased Morey Boogie, and the boards began appearing in major department stores across the United States.Morey’s invention helped establish modern bodyboarding as a sport. By the 1980s, bodyboarding had become the fastest-growing watersport in the world, according to the California Surf Museum.Today, many companies make their own versions of the bodyboard. Yet the name Morey has proved that it is difficult to replace. The museum notes that people still commonly call bodyboards ‘Boogie boards', much as brand names such as Band-Aid, Coke, Kleenex and Vaseline have become part of everyday language.

What fishers should do after catching a suspected black carp

Texas is offering $100 for every invasive black carp caught and submitted under a multi-state programme designed to improve understanding of the species as it spreads through the Mississippi River basin. The fish has been captured in waters shared by eight states, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Missouri, and Oklahoma, neighbouring river systems, while Texas is among 27 state agencies taking part in the bounty programme. According to the Invasive Carp Regional Coordinating Committee (ICRCC), participants can receive $100 per individual black carp, with up to 10 reimbursements available each month. The programme is intended to collect specimens for research because comparatively little is known about black carp in North America. The fish live near riverbeds and feed mainly on mussels and snails, raising particular concern for freshwater species. Fishers who suspect they have caught one are urged to follow the “Keep, Cool, Call” procedure and contact state fisheries officials immediately.Black carp have been captured in shared waters involving eight states: Arkansas, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri and Tennessee.The captures have occurred primarily in sections of the lower Mississippi River, Illinois River, and Ohio River. Texas is not included among the states where captures have been recorded under the programme.The species' presence in neighbouring parts of the Mississippi River basin has made monitoring and early detection important for states participating in the programme. The ICRCC's bounty programme covers the Mississippi River basin and its sub-basins, with Texas listed among the participating states. The committee says scientists and fisheries managers are collecting information on black carp age, growth, distribution and abundance, while research is also examining their diet, reproduction, habitat use and movements.Black carp live close to the riverbed and feed mainly on mussels and snails. The committee identifies freshwater mussels as the most imperilled group of animals in North America, making information about black carp distribution and feeding behaviour important to fisheries research.Texas already classifies black carp as an exotic species that is harmful or potentially harmful. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department lists black carp, of the genus Mylopharyngodon, among prohibited exotic aquatic species. It states that possession of listed exotic aquatic species without a permit is illegal in Texas.The ICRCC advises fishers who believe they have caught a black carp to follow its “Keep, Cool, Call” procedure. The fish should be retained, the capture location recorded, and photographs taken of the head, mouth and total length. Details including the fishing gear, bait and, where possible, habitat conditions such as substrate, depth, water temperature and flow should also be recorded.The fish should then be humanely killed and kept cold on ice or in a freezer. Live possession of black carp is illegal, as the species is listed as injurious under the Lacey Act. The appropriate state agency should be contacted immediately with photographs, contact details, the capture location and information about the fishing gear and habitat.Accurate identification is important because several other fish can resemble black carp. Black carp have a long, narrow head, dark external colouring ranging from black to blue-grey and a nearly straight lateral line with a slight curve in the body. Grass carp, common carp, blue suckers and buffalo species can also be mistaken for black carp, so the agency advises fishers to use identification information before reporting a suspected capture.
